metadata.title: Students’ multicultural attitudes and the role of background characteristics

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a stage sampling procedure in Cyprus: four public secondary schools were selected (with >30% students with immigrant background), then at least five classes per school were randomly selected and all students in those classes participated. The paper does not report the use of complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the analysis is based on CFA/SEM rather than PV-based achievement estimation. Because no weight variables are mentioned, it is not possible to confirm whether population-representative weighting was applied; the authors explicitly note the sample is not nationally representative. For replication, analysts should treat the results as conditional on the school/class sample and consider whether unweighted estimates are appropriate for the intended inference.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are students’ multicultural attitudes measured via the MASQUE (Likert-scale items) and social desirability measured via the MCSDS–Form C, analyzed through CFA/SEM. These are not cognitive achievement scores with Plausible Values (PV) as in ILSA achievement domains, so PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data handling strategy (e.g., listwise deletion, imputation), which is a reporting gap for transparency, especially because CFA/SEM typically requires explicit treatment of missing responses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Stage sampling in Cyprus: four public secondary schools were selected specifically because they had relatively high diversity in immigrant background (>30% students with immigrant background). Within each school, at least five classes were randomly selected and all students in those classes participated. The analytic sample comprises 450 students in 7th and 8th grade (41.8% 7th grade; 58.2% 8th grade). The paper does not report additional exclusions (e.g., missing-item thresholds) or any missing-data rule.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS (not used); Cyprus secondary schools (7th–8th grade) MASQUE multicultural attitudes (Know, Care, Act)
main_findings.target_variable: Multicultural attitudes (MASQUE factors: Know, Care, Act)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Structural regression (SEM): Gender effects—Know β=.44 (p<.001, R2=.19), Care β=.35 (p<.001, R2=.13), Act β=.37 (p<.001, R2=.14); Cohen’s d=.969, .756, .796. Model fit: χ²(95)=121.94*; CFI=.962; RMSEA=.026; SRMR=.040. Immigrant background and language: no statistically significant effects.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Cyprus secondary-school MASQUE data (7th–8th grade) on multicultural attitudes, the study leveraged Gender, Immigrant background, and Language spoken at home to model the Know, Care, and Act factors, finding that immigrant background and home language had no statistically significant effects while gender had significant medium-to-large positive effects for females across all three factors. This indicates that multicultural-attitude interventions in similar school contexts may need to be gender-responsive (especially engaging male students) rather than primarily targeting immigrant-status or home-language differences, while noting that the study is cross-sectional and not nationally representative.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS (not used); Cyprus secondary schools (7th–8th grade) MCSDS social desirability (latent factor)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Structural regression (SEM): Gender effect β=.27 (p<.001, R2=.07); Cohen’s d=.566. Model fit: χ²(54)=70.337; CFI=.960; RMSEA=.026; WRMR=.877. Immigrant background and language: no statistically significant effects.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Cyprus secondary-school MCSDS data (7th–8th grade) on social desirability bias, the study leveraged Gender, Immigrant background, and Language spoken at home to predict the social desirability construct, finding that immigrant background and home language were not significant while gender showed a significant positive association (females higher). This indicates that when interpreting self-reported multicultural attitudes, educators and researchers should consider gender-related response tendencies that may inflate or mask differences, while recognizing the study’s cross-sectional design and lack of reported missing-data handling.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS (not used); Cyprus secondary schools (7th–8th grade) MASQUE–MCSDS relationship
main_findings.target_variable: Association between social desirability and multicultural attitudes (MASQUE factors)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Final structural model: social desirability correlated positively with Care and Act—β=.34 (p<.05) for Care and β=.43 (p<.01) for Act; constrained Know–social desirability to zero. Model fit: χ²(310)=429.640; CFI=.904; RMSEA=.029; WRMR=1.016. MASQUE factor correlations ranged from .48 to .73 (p<.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Cyprus secondary-school MASQUE and MCSDS data (7th–8th grade), the study leveraged Gender and social desirability to examine how response bias relates to multicultural attitudes, finding that social desirability was positively and moderately associated with the Care and Act dimensions but not with the Know dimension. This indicates that researchers and schools should treat self-reported affective/behavioral multicultural attitudes as potentially more susceptible to socially desirable responding than cognitive knowledge components, which can inform instrument use and interpretation in evaluation and intervention studies.

data.outcome_summary: This study used a Cyprus secondary-school sample (n=450; 7th–8th grade) to validate and apply the adapted Greek Munroe Multicultural Attitude Scale Questionnaire (MASQUE) and to examine how students’ background characteristics relate to multicultural attitudes and social desirability bias. The analysis relied on CFA and SEM (not ML prediction), testing MASQUE’s three-factor structure (Know, Care, Act) and measurement invariance across gender, immigrant background, and home language, and then estimating structural paths. Gender was the only background characteristic with significant effects: females reported higher multicultural attitudes across all three MASQUE factors (e.g., Know β=.44, R2=.19) and slightly higher social desirability (β=.27, R2=.07). Immigrant background and home language showed no significant effects. Social desirability correlated positively with Care and Act (β=.34 and .43) but not with Know, suggesting response bias is more relevant for affective/behavioral components. Limitations include cross-sectional design, non-national representativeness, and no reported missing-data handling strategy.
